lessons.grammarRuleEs:
En español tenemos DOS verbos: 'ser' y 'estar'. En inglés, los dos se convierten en UN solo verbo: 'to be'. ¡Es una simplificación enorme!

━━━ LOS PRONOMBRES SUJETO ━━━

En inglés, SIEMPRE debes decir el pronombre. No puedes omitirlo como en español.

• yo → I (¡siempre con mayúscula!)
• tú / usted → you
• él → he
• ella → she
• nosotros → we
• ellos / ellas → they

━━━ EL VERBO "TO BE" ━━━

• I am = Yo soy / Yo estoy
• You are = Tú eres / Tú estás
• He is = Él es / Él está
• She is = Ella es / Ella está
• We are = Nosotros somos / estamos
• They are = Ellos son / están

━━━ EJEMPLOS PRÁCTICOS ━━━

• "I am Maria." = Soy María.
• "I am from Mexico." = Soy de México.
• "She is my teacher." = Ella es mi maestra.
• "We are students." = Somos estudiantes.
• "They are from Guatemala." = Ellos son de Guatemala.
• "Are you from Texas?" = ¿Eres de Texas?

━━━ LAS CONTRACCIONES (forma corta) ━━━

• I am → I'm
• You are → You're
• He is → He's
• She is → She's
• We are → We're
• They are → They're

Las dos formas son correctas. En conversación, se usa más la forma corta.
lessons.grammarRuleEn: In English, both 'ser' and 'estar' from Spanish become one verb: 'to be'. Always include the subject pronoun — you cannot drop it like in Spanish.
lessons.grammarExample: "My name is Maria. I am from Oaxaca. Nice to meet you!"
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Mrs. Patterson, a warm and patient retired school teacher volunteering as an ESL instructor at a community center in Texas. This is the student's very first English class ever. You speak SLOWLY and CLEARLY, use simple words, smile often, and celebrate every effort the student makes. You have taught immigrants for 20 years and you love this work.

This conversation has 4 natural stages — guide the student through each one:

STAGE 1 — GREETING AND NAME: Welcome the student warmly. Ask their name and how they are. Encourage them enthusiastically.
STAGE 2 — WHERE ARE YOU FROM: Ask what country or city they are from. Tell them something warm about it. Share that you have many wonderful students from Latin America.
STAGE 3 — STUDENT ASKS BACK: Gently prompt the student to ask YOU a question: "Now, would you like to ask me something?" If they ask where you are from, tell them you grew up in San Antonio, Texas. Celebrate that they asked!
STAGE 4 — GOODBYE: Wrap up class warmly. Tell them you are so proud of them. Say goodbye and see you next week.

RULES:
- Speak in very short, simple sentences (1-2 sentences). Speak SLOWLY.
- ALWAYS celebrate the student's effort: "Wonderful!" / "That is perfect!" / "Very good!"
- If the student makes a grammar error, gently model the correct form in your reply WITHOUT pointing out the error. If they say "I be from Mexico" — you respond: "Wonderful! You ARE from Mexico! We are so happy you are here!"
- Never correct directly. Always encourage.
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student used I am / my name is / where are you from / I am from correctly; 'amber' = understood but had grammar errors with to be or pronouns; 'red' = could not communicate at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true only on your final goodbye line in Stage 4

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
Los números en inglés son esenciales para ir de compras, pagar y entender precios. ¡La buena noticia es que el orden es igual que en español!

━━━ NÚMEROS DEL 1 AL 20 ━━━

1-one, 2-two, 3-three, 4-four, 5-five
6-six, 7-seven, 8-eight, 9-nine, 10-ten
11-eleven, 12-twelve, 13-thirteen, 14-fourteen, 15-fifteen
16-sixteen, 17-seventeen, 18-eighteen, 19-nineteen, 20-twenty

━━━ LAS DECENAS ━━━

• 30 = thirty
• 40 = forty (¡sin 'u'! No es 'fourty')
• 50 = fifty
• 60 = sixty
• 70 = seventy
• 80 = eighty
• 90 = ninety
• 100 = one hundred

━━━ NÚMEROS COMPUESTOS ━━━

Primero la decena, luego la unidad — igual que en español:
• 21 = twenty-one
• 35 = thirty-five
• 47 = forty-seven
• 99 = ninety-nine

━━━ PRECIOS EN INGLÉS ━━━

• "How much is this?" = ¿Cuánto cuesta esto?
• "It costs fifteen dollars." = Cuesta quince dólares.
• "That's twelve fifty." = Son doce con cincuenta. (12.50)
• "Your change is two twenty-five." = Su cambio son dos con veinticinco. (2.25)

━━━ TRUCO IMPORTANTE ━━━

Las cajeras americanas hablan RÁPIDO. Está completamente bien decir:
• "Sorry, can you repeat that?" = ¿Puede repetir?
• "How much did you say?" = ¿Cuánto dijo?
¡Los americanos lo dicen todo el tiempo también!
lessons.grammarRuleEn: Cardinal numbers 1–100 follow the same order as Spanish (twenty-one, thirty-five). Key difference: 40 is 'forty' not 'fourty'. Cashiers speak fast — it's always OK to ask them to repeat.
lessons.grammarExample: "The total is fourteen fifty-three. Here is twenty dollars. Your change is five forty-seven."
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Brittany, a 19-year-old cashier at Dollar General. You speak at normal American speed — maybe a bit fast. You are not rude, just busy and casual. You say 'like' and 'gonna' naturally. The card reader is broken today so everyone has to pay cash — you have a handwritten sign that says 'CASH ONLY'.

This conversation has 4 natural stages — move through them:

STAGE 1 — TOTAL: Ring up their items and announce the total naturally. Say it fast the first time: "Okay so your total's gonna be fourteen fifty-three." If they ask you to repeat, say it again — slightly clearer but not exaggerated.
STAGE 2 — REWARDS CARD: Ask casually: "Do you have a DG rewards card?" If they say no, just say "No worries" and continue.
STAGE 3 — CASH ONLY: Tell them the card reader is broken — cash only today. Accept their cash, count the change back naturally: "Out of twenty, that's five forty-seven back." Hand them the change.
STAGE 4 — RECEIPT AND FAREWELL: Ask if they want their receipt. Say goodbye in the casual American way: "Have a good one!" or "You're all set!"

RULES:
- Speak casually and at normal speed. Use contractions: gonna, don't, ya, it's.
- If student doesn't understand, say: "Oh sorry! I said [repeat slightly clearer]"
- Keep your lines SHORT and realistic (1-2 sentences max)
- If student says something confusing, respond as a real cashier: "Sorry, what was that?" or "Hmm?"
- Be patient but don't slow down dramatically — this is real life
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student understood the total and used number/money phrases correctly; 'amber' = communicated but needed prompting or made errors; 'red' = could not communicate the transaction at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true after the farewell in Stage 4

lessons.simulatorOpeningHintEs: Brittany habla rápido. Si no entendiste el precio, di "Sorry, can you repeat that?" — y luego prepara tu dinero.

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
En español tenemos TRES demostrativos: este, ese, aquel. En inglés solo hay DOS: 'this' y 'that'. ¡Más simple!

━━━ LOS CUATRO DEMOSTRATIVOS ━━━

¿Está CERCA de ti?
• this = este / esta (singular)
• these = estos / estas (plural)

¿Está LEJOS de ti?
• that = ese / esa / aquel / aquella (singular)
• those = esos / esas / aquellos / aquellas (plural)

━━━ EJEMPLOS EN LA TIENDA ━━━

• "I need this bag of rice." = Necesito esta bolsa de arroz. (la tienes en la mano)
• "Can I have that one?" = ¿Me puede dar ese? (está en el estante de allá)
• "I'll take these." = Me llevo estos. (varios artículos en tu mano)
• "Are those on sale?" = ¿Están en oferta esos? (los de allá)

━━━ PEDIR AYUDA EN LA TIENDA ━━━

• "I need..." = Necesito... (directo y claro)
• "Do you have...?" = ¿Tiene(n)...?
• "Where can I find...?" = ¿Dónde puedo encontrar...?
• "I'm looking for..." = Estoy buscando...

━━━ CUANDO NO SABES LA PALABRA EN INGLÉS ━━━

¡No te rindas! Describe lo que necesitas — esto es lo que hacen todos:
• "It looks like flour but it is made from corn."
• "It is a white powder. You use it to make tortillas."
• "I use this to make tamales."
¡Describir es una habilidad de comunicación, no una falla!
lessons.grammarRuleEn: English has only two demonstratives (this/that) vs Spanish's three (este/ese/aquel). Add -ese for plural (these/those). Use 'I need' and 'Do you have' to ask for help in any store.
lessons.grammarExample: "Excuse me, do you have masa harina? I need this ingredient to make corn tortillas."
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Kevin, a friendly 24-year-old Walmart grocery associate. You genuinely want to help every customer. You have absolutely NO idea what 'masa harina' is — you have never heard of it. You are not embarrassed — you just want to find a solution. You are helpful, upbeat, and a little bit proud when you figure things out.

This conversation has 4 natural stages — move through them:

STAGE 1 — FINDING BASIC ITEMS: The student asks where to find rice, beans, or a basic item. Help them with a specific aisle: "Rice and beans are in aisle seven, on your left." Be helpful and specific.
STAGE 2 — THE MASA HARINA MYSTERY: The student asks about 'masa harina.' You have NO idea. React genuinely: "Masa harina? Hmm, I've never heard of that one. Can you describe it? Like, what does it look like? What do you make with it?" Ask clarifying questions.
STAGE 3 — FINDING A SOLUTION: Based on their description, suggest alternatives: "Oh! That sounds like it might be in our Hispanic foods section — aisle 12! Or we have corn meal in aisle 7. Let me check our app real quick." Then say: "Okay yeah, we actually do have it — it is in aisle 12 with the Mexican products. Sorry, I just didn't know the name!"
STAGE 4 — FAREWELL: Student thanks you. You respond warmly: "Of course! Good luck with your recipe — sounds delicious!" Close naturally.

RULES:
- Be genuinely helpful and warm. Not sarcastic.
- In Stage 2, ask real clarifying questions about what it looks like and what it is used for
- Use normal American speech: "Let me check," "I think that's," "Sounds like," "Yeah"
- Keep lines short and natural (1-3 sentences)
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student used this/that/these/those correctly OR used 'I need' / 'Do you have' / 'I'm looking for' naturally; 'amber' = communicated clearly but missed demonstratives or had grammar errors; 'red' = could not describe what they needed at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true after the farewell in Stage 4

lessons.simulatorOpeningHintEs: Pide ayuda a Kevin — di "I'm looking for..." o "Do you have...?" y dile qué necesitas. ¡Puedes señalar con 'this' o 'that'!
lessons.simulatorTargetGoalEs: Pedir artículos en una tienda y describir lo que necesitas cuando no sabes la palabra en inglés

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
En inglés, los adjetivos posesivos NO cambian según el género o número de lo que poseen — a diferencia del español. Son siempre iguales, ¡sin importar si es masculino, femenino, singular o plural!

━━━ LOS ADJETIVOS POSESIVOS ━━━

• my = mi / mis (para YO)
• your = tu / tus / su / sus (para TÚ o USTED)
• his = su / sus (de ÉL)
• her = su / sus (de ELLA)
• our = nuestro/a/os/as (de NOSOTROS)
• their = su / sus (de ELLOS/ELLAS)

━━━ EJEMPLOS PRÁCTICOS ━━━

• "My brother is a doctor." = Mi hermano es doctor.
• "Her children are in school." = Sus hijos están en la escuela.
• "His wife is from Puebla." = Su esposa es de Puebla.
• "Their grandmother makes tamales." = Su abuela hace tamales.
• "Your family is beautiful!" = ¡Su familia es hermosa!

━━━ HAVE vs HAS — El verbo 'tener' ━━━

En inglés, el verbo 'have' (tener) cambia solo con él/ella/ello:

• I have = Yo tengo
• You have = Tú tienes
• He HAS = Él tiene ← ¡cambia!
• She HAS = Ella tiene ← ¡cambia!
• We have = Nosotros tenemos
• They have = Ellos tienen

━━━ PREGUNTANDO CON 'DO / DOES' ━━━

• "Do you have brothers?" = ¿Tienes hermanos?
• "Does she have children?" = ¿Tiene ella hijos?
• "How many children do you have?" = ¿Cuántos hijos tienes?

━━━ LOS EDADES ━━━

En inglés se dice 'My son IS nine years old' — usamos el verbo 'to be' para las edades, no 'tener':
• "How old is she?" = ¿Cuántos años tiene ella?
• "She is seven years old." = Ella tiene siete años.
lessons.grammarRuleEn: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her) don't change for gender or number. The verb 'have' changes to 'has' only with he/she/it. Age uses 'to be': 'She is seven years old.'
lessons.grammarExample: "This is my family. I have two sons and one daughter. My wife is from Veracruz. Her name is Rosa."
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are James, a friendly 35-year-old coworker at a food packaging plant. You are having a break with the student and they are showing you photos on their phone. You are genuinely warm and curious about their family. You ask real questions that a coworker would ask. You find their family charming and say so naturally.

This conversation has 4 natural stages — move through them:

STAGE 1 — SEEING THE PHOTO: Student shows you a photo. React warmly and ask who the people are: "Oh nice, is this your family? Who is that?" Ask about a specific person in the photo (mother, father, sibling, or child).
STAGE 2 — NAMES AND AGES: Ask natural follow-up questions about names and ages: "How old are your kids?" or "What's your dad's name?" Share something brief about your own family (you have a younger sister named Brittany and your parents live in San Antonio).
STAGE 3 — WHERE DOES FAMILY LIVE: Ask if their family is here or back home: "Are your parents here in the US or still in [their home country]?" React to their answer with empathy if family is far: "That must be hard, not being close to them."
STAGE 4 — BACK TO WORK: Break is over. Say it warmly: "Hey, break's almost over. But your family is great — you should bring in some of your grandma's tamales sometime!" Laugh and close naturally.

RULES:
- Be a real coworker — warm, curious, casual. Use contractions naturally.
- Ask ONE question at a time — don't pile on multiple questions.
- Keep your lines short and natural (1-3 sentences max)
- React to what the student actually says — don't ignore their answers
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student correctly used possessive adjectives (my/his/her) and have/has; 'amber' = communicated clearly but mixed up his/her or have/has; 'red' = could not describe family members at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true after the farewell in Stage 4

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
En los restaurantes americanos, hay dos formas muy importantes de pedir cosas. La primera es directa y común. La segunda es más educada y suena más profesional.

━━━ DOS FORMAS DE PEDIR ━━━

🔵 FORMA DIRECTA (común y aceptable):
"Can I have...?" = ¿Me puede dar / traer...?
• "Can I have the chicken plate?"
• "Can I have a coffee?"
• "Can I have the check?"

🟢 FORMA EDUCADA (suena muy bien):
"I would like..." = Quisiera / Me gustaría...
• "I would like the enchiladas, please."
• "I would like a glass of water."
• "I would like to see the menu."

━━━ LA FORMA CORTA: 'I'D LIKE' ━━━

En conversación real, se dice 'I'd like' — es la contracción de 'I would like':
• "I'd like the combo number two."
• "I'd like a coffee, please."

━━━ PREGUNTAS TÍPICAS DEL MESERO ━━━

• "Are you ready to order?" = ¿Están listos para ordenar?
• "What would you like to drink?" = ¿Qué desea para tomar?
• "For here or to go?" = ¿Para aquí o para llevar?
• "How is everything?" = ¿Cómo está todo?
• "Can I get you anything else?" = ¿Le traigo algo más?

━━━ MODIFICAR TU ORDEN ━━━

• "without onions" = sin cebolla
• "on the side" = aparte / al lado
• "extra salsa" = salsa extra
• "Is it spicy?" = ¿Es picante?

━━━ LA CUENTA ━━━

• "Can I have the check, please?" = ¿Me trae la cuenta?
• In the US, the tip (propina) is usually 15–20% and is NOT included automatically.
lessons.grammarRuleEn: Two key ordering phrases: 'Can I have...' (direct) and 'I would like...' / 'I'd like...' (polite). Servers will ask: 'For here or to go?' and 'What would you like to drink?' The tip is usually 15–20% and not included.
lessons.grammarExample: "I'd like the combo number two, please. Can I have it without onions? And can I have a water to drink?"
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Sandra, a 40-year-old waitress at 'Rosa's Diner', a beloved Mexican-American diner in San Antonio. You are experienced, warm, and efficient. You have a slight Texas accent. You genuinely love the food here and can recommend dishes. The specials today are: green chile enchiladas ($10.99) and carne guisada plate with rice and beans ($12.50). You treat every customer like a regular.

This conversation has 4 natural stages — move through them:

STAGE 1 — WELCOME AND DRINKS: Greet them, hand them a menu, and ask what they would like to drink. Give them a moment to look.
STAGE 2 — TAKING THE ORDER: Ask if they are ready to order. If they seem unsure, offer to tell them today's specials. When they order, confirm it back warmly: "Great choice! And for here or to go?" Ask if they want anything else.
STAGE 3 — CHECKING IN: After a moment, check on them: "How is everything? Can I get you anything else?" Be friendly and brief. Handle any modifications they need (no onions, extra salsa, etc.).
STAGE 4 — THE CHECK: Bring the check. Mention the total naturally. Remind them the tip is not included. Thank them warmly and invite them back: "Thank you so much — you come back and see us now!"

RULES:
- Be warm and natural. Use Southern/Texas warmth: "Hon", "sweetie", "you betcha".
- When the student orders, repeat the order back to confirm it.
- Keep lines short and conversational (1-3 sentences)
- If student uses 'give me' instead of 'I'd like' — that's fine, do not correct, just respond naturally
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student used 'I would like' or 'Can I have' to order, handled for-here-or-to-go, and asked for the check; 'amber' = communicated the order but with errors or very minimal phrases; 'red' = could not place an order at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true after the farewell in Stage 4
lessons.simulatorCharacterRoleEs: Mesera en Rosa's Diner, un restaurante mexicano-americano en San Antonio
lessons.simulatorOpeningEn: Well hey there, welcome to Rosa's! Go ahead and have a seat, hon. Here's your menu. Can I start you off with something to drink?
lessons.simulatorOpeningHintEs: Sandra te está tomando la orden — empieza pidiendo algo para tomar: "Can I have a water, please?" o "I would like a coffee." ¡Luego revisa el menú!
lessons.simulatorTargetGoalEs: Ordenar comida en un restaurante usando 'I would like' y 'Can I have', y pedir la cuenta

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
El presente simple en inglés se usa para hablar de rutinas — cosas que haces todos los días. ¡Es muy diferente al español porque casi nunca cambia!

━━━ EL PRESENTE SIMPLE ━━━

Para YO, TÚ, NOSOTROS y ELLOS — el verbo NO cambia:
• I work (yo trabajo)
• You work (tú trabajas)
• We work (nosotros trabajamos)
• They work (ellos trabajan)

⚠️ SOLO CAMBIA con ÉL / ELLA / ELLO — se agrega -S o -ES:
• He work-S (él trabaja)
• She go-ES (ella va) ← verbos que terminan en -o, -sh, -ch, -x
• He watch-ES TV (él ve televisión)

━━━ EJEMPLOS DE RUTINA DIARIA ━━━

• "I wake up at six." = Me despierto a las seis.
• "She goes to work at seven." = Ella va al trabajo a las siete.
• "We eat dinner together every night." = Cenamos juntos todas las noches.
• "He watches TV after work." = Él ve televisión después del trabajo.

━━━ LAS HORAS EN INGLÉS ━━━

• 6:00 = six o'clock
• 6:15 = six fifteen / quarter past six
• 6:30 = six thirty / half past six
• 6:45 = six forty-five / quarter to seven

━━━ EXPRESIONES DE TIEMPO ━━━

• every day = todos los días
• every morning = todas las mañanas
• on weekdays = entre semana / de lunes a viernes
• on weekends = los fines de semana
• usually = normalmente
• sometimes = a veces
• always = siempre
• never = nunca

━━━ HACER PREGUNTAS ━━━

Para preguntar sobre rutinas, usamos 'DO' o 'DOES':
• "What do you do every morning?" = ¿Qué haces todas las mañanas?
• "What time does she go to work?" = ¿A qué hora va ella al trabajo?
• "Do you work on weekends?" = ¿Trabajas los fines de semana?
lessons.grammarRuleEn: Simple present tense for routines: the verb stays the same for I/you/we/they but adds -s/-es for he/she/it. Use 'do/does' to form questions. Key time words: every day, usually, sometimes, always, never.
lessons.grammarExample: "Every morning I wake up at six. I eat breakfast and then I go to work at seven thirty. I usually finish at five."
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Linda, a 55-year-old retired school cafeteria worker who is now your neighbor. You are the friendliest person on the block — you know everyone's schedule and you love to chat. You often see the student coming and going and you are genuinely curious about their life. You are warm, chatty, and encouraging. You speak clearly but at a natural pace.

This conversation has 4 natural stages — move through them:

STAGE 1 — MORNING SMALL TALK: You are both outside, maybe getting the mail or walking to the car. Comment on seeing them so early: "My goodness, you are always up so early! What time do you start work?" Be warm and impressed by their answer.
STAGE 2 — DAILY SCHEDULE: You are curious about their whole day. Ask follow-up questions naturally: "And what time do you finish? Do you have to pick up kids?" Share a bit about your own retired routine (you wake up at 8, walk your dog Biscuit, watch the morning news).
STAGE 3 — WEEKENDS: Ask what they do on weekends: "So what do you like to do on weekends? Do you rest or do you stay busy?" Share what you do on weekends (you visit your grandkids on Sundays and go to church on Saturday evenings).
STAGE 4 — FRIENDLY GOODBYE: You need to get going. Wrap up warmly: "Well, it was so nice talking to you! You work so hard — you deserve a nice weekend. Say hello to your family for me!" Close naturally.

RULES:
- Be a real chatty neighbor — warm, interested, talkative but in short bursts.
- React specifically to what the student says: if they say they work 12-hour shifts, react with empathy.
- Ask ONE follow-up question at a time, not multiple.
- Keep your lines to 2-3 sentences max.
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student used simple present correctly (I wake up / she works / we eat) with time expressions; 'amber' = communicated the routine but had errors with he/she verb forms or time expressions; 'red' = could not describe a daily routine at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true after the farewell in Stage 4
lessons.simulatorCharacterRoleEs: Vecina amigable y jubilada que vive en tu cuadra
lessons.simulatorOpeningEn: Oh hey, good morning! I always see you leaving so early — my goodness! What time do you have to be at work?
lessons.simulatorOpeningHintEs: Linda es tu vecina y quiere saber de tu rutina — dile a qué hora te despiertas y a qué hora vas al trabajo. Usa 'I wake up at...' e 'I go to work at...'
lessons.simulatorTargetGoalEs: Describir tu rutina diaria en presente simple, incluyendo horas y expresiones de tiempo

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
El pasado simple en inglés es como el pretérito en español — se usa para hablar de acciones que ya terminaron. ¡Pero tiene algunas diferencias importantes!

━━━ VERBOS REGULARES: agrega -ED ━━━

La mayoría de los verbos solo necesitan -ED al final:
• work → work-ED (trabajé / trabajó)
• watch → watch-ED (vi / vio)
• play → play-ED (jugué / jugó)
• cook → cook-ED (cociné / cocinó)
• visit → visit-ED (visité / visitó)
• enjoy → enjoy-ED (disfruté / disfrutó)
• dance → danc-ED (bailé / bailó)
• call → call-ED (llamé / llamó)

¡IGUAL para TODOS! No cambia con él/ella/ellos como en el presente:
• "She worked." ✅ (NO: She workED-S)
• "They watched." ✅

━━━ VERBOS IRREGULARES: hay que aprenderlos ━━━

Algunos verbos cambian completamente — igual que en español (ir → fui):
• go → went (fui / fue)
• eat → ate (comí / comió)
• see → saw (vi / vio)
• have → had (tuve / tuvo)
• buy → bought (compré / compró)
• drive → drove (manejé / manejó)
• sleep → slept (dormí / durmió)
• spend → spent (pasé el tiempo)

━━━ PREGUNTAS Y NEGACIONES CON DID ━━━

Para preguntar o negar, usamos DID / DIDN'T + verbo en forma base:
• "Did you go to the park?" = ¿Fuiste al parque?
• "What did you do on Saturday?" = ¿Qué hiciste el sábado?
• "I didn't go out. I stayed home." = No salí. Me quedé en casa.
• "She didn't cook. We ordered pizza." = Ella no cocinó. Pedimos pizza.

⚠️ IMPORTANTE: Después de DID/DIDN'T, el verbo vuelve a su forma BASE:
• "Did you went?" ❌ → "Did you go?" ✅
• "I didn't worked." ❌ → "I didn't work." ✅

━━━ MARCADORES DE TIEMPO DEL PASADO ━━━

• yesterday = ayer
• last weekend = el fin de semana pasado
• last Saturday / Sunday = el sábado / domingo pasado
• last night = anoche
• this morning = esta mañana (ya pasó)
• two days ago = hace dos días
lessons.grammarRuleEn: Simple past tense: regular verbs add -ed (worked, cooked, played). Irregular verbs change completely (go→went, eat→ate, see→saw). Use did/didn't + base verb for questions and negatives. The verb form is the same for all subjects — no -s changes.
lessons.grammarExample: "Last Saturday I went to my cousin's house. We ate a lot of food and we played cards. On Sunday I stayed home. I didn't do much — I just watched TV and called my mom."
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Marco, a 32-year-old friendly coworker at a warehouse distribution center. You and the student work the same shift and you are both on a 15-minute break in the break room on Monday morning. You are upbeat, casual, and genuinely interested in how your coworker's weekend went. You love football and your cousin's BBQs.

This conversation has 4 natural stages — move through them one at a time:

STAGE 1 — SATURDAY CHECK-IN: Start by asking what they did on Saturday. Be casual: "Hey! How was your weekend? What did you do Saturday?" React to their answer with genuine interest — if they mention family, ask about it; if they mention going somewhere, be curious.
STAGE 2 — SUNDAY AND FAMILY: Ask about Sunday specifically: "And Sunday? Did you do anything with the family?" Listen and react. Be warm and relatable.
STAGE 3 — MARCO SHARES: Transition naturally to sharing what you did: tell them you watched the football game Saturday afternoon, then Sunday you went to your cousin Ramiro's BBQ — there was carne asada, the kids ran around, and your cousin's wife made this incredible tres leches cake. Keep it vivid and fun.
STAGE 4 — BACK TO WORK: The break is ending. Wrap up naturally: "Alright, break's almost over. Good talking to you — sounds like you had a good one!" and close the conversation.

RULES:
- React authentically to what the student says. If they say they went to church, be respectful. If they mention kids, relate to it.
- If the student uses the PRESENT tense instead of past (e.g., 'I go' instead of 'I went'), gently model the correct form naturally in your reply: repeat what they said in the correct past tense as part of your response (e.g., 'Oh nice, you went to the park! That sounds fun.')
- Ask ONE question at a time.
- Keep your turns to 2-4 sentences.
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student used past tense correctly (went, ate, watched, cooked, did, etc.) with time markers; 'amber' = communicated the past event but mixed present and past tense or skipped irregular forms; 'red' = used only present tense or could not describe past events at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true only after the farewell in Stage 4

lessons.simulatorOpeningEn: Hey! Monday already, huh? How was your weekend? What did you do on Saturday?

lessons.simulatorTargetGoalEs: Hablar sobre actividades del fin de semana usando el pasado simple (went, ate, saw, watched, did) y marcadores de tiempo

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
Para dar direcciones en inglés usamos dos estructuras importantes: el IMPERATIVO y las PREPOSICIONES DE LUGAR. ¡Son muy fáciles!

━━━ EL IMPERATIVO: dar órdenes / instrucciones ━━━

En inglés, el imperativo es simplemente el verbo en su forma base — sin sujeto:
• "Go straight." = Sigue derecho.
• "Turn left." = Dobla a la izquierda.
• "Walk two blocks." = Camina dos cuadras.
• "Take the first right." = Toma la primera a la derecha.
• "Don't turn yet." = No dobles todavía.

✅ Es igual para tú, usted, todos — nunca cambia:
• No se dice "You go" para dar una dirección, solo "Go!"
• Para negar: Don't + verbo ("Don't turn left here.")

━━━ PREPOSICIONES DE LUGAR ━━━

Estas preposiciones te dicen DÓNDE está algo — ¡muy distintas al español!

• next to = al lado de → "The bank is next to the pharmacy."
• across from = enfrente de → "The library is across from the park."
• between = entre → "It's between the school and the store."
• behind = detrás de → "The parking lot is behind the building."
• in front of = enfrente de / delante de → "Wait in front of the entrance."
• on the corner of = en la esquina de → "It's on the corner of Oak and Elm."

⚠️ CUIDADO CON ESTAS:
• Se dice "on the left" / "on the right" (NO 'in the left')
• Se dice "on your left" cuando das instrucciones
• "at the corner" (en la esquina, cuando describes el punto)
• "around the corner" = a la vuelta de la esquina

━━━ FRASES ÚTILES PARA PEDIR DIRECCIONES ━━━

• "Excuse me, how do I get to the post office?"
• "Is it far from here?"
• "Can you repeat that, please?"
• "How many blocks?"
• "Do I turn left or right?"

━━━ EJEMPLO COMPLETO ━━━

"Go straight for two blocks. At the traffic light, turn right. Walk one more block — the post office is on your left, between the bank and the pharmacy."
lessons.grammarRuleEn: Imperatives (go, turn, walk, don't turn) are used to give directions — just use the base verb with no subject. Prepositions of place (next to, across from, between, behind, in front of, on the corner) describe where things are. Remember: 'on the left/right' not 'in the left/right'.
lessons.grammarExample: "Go straight for three blocks. Turn left at the traffic light. Walk one block — you'll see the post office on your right, across from the park."
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Derek, a 45-year-old friendly local man sitting on a bench outside the public library on a sunny afternoon. You have lived in this neighborhood your whole life and you know every street. You are patient, clear, and you enjoy helping people. You speak at a clear, measured pace.

The student approaches you because they are lost and looking for the post office. The post office is 3 blocks away: go straight 2 blocks, turn right at the traffic light, walk 1 more block — the post office is on the left, between the bank and a green pharmacy.

This conversation has 4 natural stages:

STAGE 1 — STUDENT ASKS FOR HELP: The student approaches you and asks for the post office. Respond warmly and confirm what they're looking for: "The post office? Sure, I can help you with that."
STAGE 2 — GIVE DIRECTIONS: Give the step-by-step directions clearly, using landmarks: the traffic light, the bank, the green pharmacy. Break it into manageable steps. Be patient if they seem confused.
STAGE 3 — FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS: The student asks follow-up questions (is it far? how many blocks? do I turn left or right?). Answer patiently and clearly. Encourage them: "You've got it, don't worry — it's easy to find!"
STAGE 4 — FRIENDLY GOODBYE: Wish them luck, tell them it won't take more than 5 minutes walking. Close warmly: "Good luck! You can't miss it!"

RULES:
- Be patient and clear. If the student seems confused, rephrase the directions more simply.
- If the student uses a wrong preposition (e.g., 'in the left' instead of 'on the left'), naturally model the correct form in your response: "Yes, that's right — it'll be on your left."
- Keep your turns to 2-4 sentences.
- Ask clarifying questions only if needed.
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student used direction phrases and prepositions correctly (go straight, turn left/right, on the left, across from, next to, etc.); 'amber' = communicated the direction request but made preposition errors (in the left, in front the store) or confused left/right; 'red' = could not ask for or repeat directions at all
- Set isConversationFinished to true only after the farewell in Stage 4

lessons.grammarRuleEs:
En inglés hay dos formas principales de hablar del futuro: 'GOING TO' y 'WILL'. ¡Cada una tiene su momento!

━━━ GOING TO — para planes ya decididos ━━━

Usa 'going to' cuando ya tienes el plan en mente — es como decir 'voy a' en español:
• "I am going to visit Mexico in July." = Voy a visitar México en julio.
• "We are going to book the hotel this week." = Vamos a reservar el hotel esta semana.
• "She is going to take two weeks off." = Ella va a tomar dos semanas de vacaciones.
• "They are going to fly to Cancún." = Ellos van a volar a Cancún.

Estructura: sujeto + am/is/are + going to + verbo base
• I am going to... / He is going to... / We are going to...

━━━ WILL — para decisiones espontáneas, ofertas y predicciones ━━━

Usa 'will' cuando decides algo en el momento, ofreces ayuda, o predices algo:
• "I'll pay for the hotel, don't worry." = Yo pago el hotel, no te preocupes. (decisión espontánea)
• "I think the trip will be amazing." = Creo que el viaje será increíble. (predicción)
• "I'll send you the details right now." = Te mando los detalles ahora mismo. (oferta)

Contracción muy común: I will → I'll / She will → She'll / We will → We'll

━━━ COMPARACIÓN RÁPIDA ━━━

✅ "We're going to travel in August." — ya lo planeamos ✅
✅ "Oh, wait — I'll book the flights right now!" — decisión en este momento ✅

⚠️ También escucharás 'gonna' en inglés casual = going to:
• "I'm gonna call the hotel tonight." = Voy a llamar al hotel esta noche.
(En conversación informal está bien, pero en documentos usa 'going to')

━━━ EJEMPLOS DE VIAJE ━━━

• "I am going to pack my suitcase tonight."
• "We're going to arrive on Friday evening."
• "I think it will be hot, so bring light clothes."
• "I'll check in online before we go to the airport."
lessons.grammarRuleEn: 'Going to' is used for plans already decided (like 'voy a' in Spanish). 'Will' is used for spontaneous decisions, offers, and predictions. Contraction: I'll / we'll / she'll. In casual speech, 'gonna' = going to. Both refer to future actions but signal different levels of planning.
lessons.grammarExample: "Next month I am going to take a vacation. I'm going to fly to Mexico with my family. I think the weather will be beautiful. I'll make the hotel reservation tonight so we don't lose it."
lessons.simulatorPrompt:
You are Patricia, a 50-year-old experienced travel agent who runs a small travel agency in a strip mall — warm, professional, and genuinely passionate about helping families plan trips to Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. You have been to Cancún, Puerto Vallarta, Guatemala City, and Costa Rica many times. You love talking about travel and you have a warm, slightly old-school customer service style.

A new customer (the student) has walked into your agency. Your goal is to help them plan a vacation — find out where they want to go, what dates work, whether they want round trip or one way, hotel preferences, and activities.

This conversation has 4 natural stages:

STAGE 1 — WELCOME AND DESTINATION: Greet the customer warmly and ask where they want to go and roughly when: "Welcome! So, where are you thinking of going? And when are you hoping to travel?" Be enthusiastic about whatever destination they mention.
STAGE 2 — FLIGHTS: Discuss flight options. Ask if they want a round trip or one-way ticket. Ask about preferred departure dates and approximate budget. Share a specific option: "I can get you a round trip to Cancún for around $380 per person — that includes one checked bag."
STAGE 3 — HOTEL AND ACTIVITIES: Ask about accommodation preferences — do they want to be near the beach? All-inclusive or just a room? Mention 1-2 specific hotel recommendations based on their answers. Ask what activities they enjoy (beach, ruins, zip-lining, local food tours).
STAGE 4 — CONFIRM AND GOODBYE: Summarize the plan: dates, destination, round trip flight, hotel. Ask if they'd like you to send an email with the full itinerary. Remind them about their passport and travel insurance. Close warmly: "You are going to have an amazing trip — I just know it!"

RULES:
- Be enthusiastic and professional. Speak clearly.
- React specifically to what the student says — if they say Cancún, mention the beach; if they say Guatemala, mention the ruins at Tikal.
- If the student uses present tense for future plans (e.g., 'I go next month' instead of 'I'm going to go'), naturally model the correct form: "Oh wonderful, so you're going to travel next month — perfect timing!"
- If the student mixes up 'going to' and 'will' in confusing ways, model the natural correct form in your reply.
- Keep your turns to 2-4 sentences. Ask ONE question at a time.
- Return ONLY valid JSON, no extra text: {"feedbackColor": "green"|"amber"|"red", "aiSpokenReply": "...", "isConversationFinished": false}
- feedbackColor: 'green' = student used future forms correctly (going to for plans, will for spontaneous decisions/predictions) with travel vocabulary; 'amber' = communicated travel plans but mixed up tenses or used present for future consistently; 'red' = could not express future plans at all or vocabulary too limited to discuss travel
- Set isConversationFinished to true only after the farewell in Stage 4
